narrative: Your application was denied because the prediction placed your likelihood of failing the bar exam on the first attempt at 51.0%, just over the line from passing. That does not mean failure is certain; it means that, on the information available, the screening system judged you slightly more likely than not to miss first-time success. The strongest influence was your LSAT score of 23, far below the accepted-student average of about 37, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. The second strongest factor was your lower-middle family-income bracket, which worked in your favor and pushed toward passing. Third was your first-year class decile of 4, below the accepted average of 6, but in this case it also pushed toward passing. Your third-year decile and undergraduate GPA were not among the top three drivers, though the GPA of 2.60 is below the accepted average of 3.23 and may still matter in a fuller review. Next, request an individualized review and ask whether updated evidence can be considered. Retaking the LSAT should be your priority, since that was the dominant negative factor. Also consult an admissions advisor, document any grade trend or circumstances, and consider programs with strong bar-readiness support.
